title: ShinyHunters hacks Clop leak site and threatens to extort the extortionists
content_md:
ShinyHunters hacks Clop leak site and threatens to extort the extortionists

Overnight between Friday and Saturday, the data leak site of Clop (or Cl0p), one of the most lethal ransomware groups of recent years, was breached and defaced. Not by an international task force, not by a security vendor, but by another extortion gang: ShinyHunters. The collective uploaded a taunting file, then replaced the entire page with the ASCII art of Umbreon, its historic signature, accompanied by the message "rooting your systems since '19 ;)". Now ShinyHunters is threatening to publish the stolen data if Clop does not pay within 72 hours.

The two groups have history. According to ShinyHunters' account, the exploit behind Clop's October 2025 Oracle E-Business Suite campaign (CVE-2025-61882) was originally developed by ShinyHunters or the broader Scattered Lapsus$ Hunters collective, then obtained by Clop without authorization and used for large-scale extortion. The situation escalated: a Clop representative allegedly threatened ShinyHunters in Russian, with physical threats, motivating Saturday's attack.

Technically, the intrusion was straightforward. ShinyHunters exploited an unauthenticated file upload vulnerability in Grav CMS, the content management system running Clop's Tor infrastructure. They uploaded a provocative text file reading "THIS SITE HAS BEEN PWN3D BY SHINYHUNTERES #Skids10p -- Maybe don't try to threaten us next time," followed by a complete defacement with Umbreon ASCII art. According to ShinyHunters' statements to BleepingComputer, the haul included Grav CMS source code and plugins, system logs from /var/log (potentially containing authentication data and visitor IP addresses), and critically, the Tor onion service's private cryptographic keys. Possession of those keys would theoretically allow running Clop's existing .onion address on servers controlled by ShinyHunters.

ShinyHunters has openly declared its intent: "Going to extort them" -- applying the same business model against Clop that the group normally uses against corporate victims. Clop has 72 hours to contact ShinyHunters before the stolen data is published publicly.

For defenders, the episode offers several takeaways. Even the most established criminal infrastructure can have trivial attack surfaces -- in this case a CMS with a known upload vulnerability. If Clop's Tor service keys are truly compromised, organizations previously victimized by Clop should consider "double exposure" risk if ShinyHunters decides to release data that Clop had stolen but never published. Internal frictions between extortion groups can generate valuable intelligence -- logs, credentials, internal chats -- that researchers and law enforcement can exploit, as has happened with leaked chats from other ransomware gangs.

Timeline:
- October 2025: Clop exploits CVE-2025-61882 (Oracle E-Business Suite) for large-scale extortion campaign
- October 2025: ShinyHunters/Scattered Lapsus$ Hunters distribute a PoC of the exploit, claiming authorship
- 2026: Tensions escalate, direct threats from an alleged Clop member
- September 19, 2026: ShinyHunters exploits unauthenticated file upload in Grav CMS on Clop's Tor leak site
- September 19, 2026: Provocative text file uploaded, followed by full defacement (Umbreon ASCII art)
- Claimed data: Grav CMS source code and plugins, /var/log logs, Tor onion service private keys
- Threat: Data publication within 72 hours if Clop does not pay
- Exploited vulnerability: Unauthenticated file upload in Grav CMS
